issues.legal_issue: Environmental decision-makers must apply a precautionary approach where uncertain science leaves a threat of serious or irreversible environmental harm.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a proposed industrial facility in a sensitive catchment area supplying drinking water to nearby cities.
The parties presented conflicting technical opinions about the facility’s pollution potential and the adequacy of its safeguards.
The court recognized that environmental science may be uncertain and that harm may become irreversible before its effects can be established.
issues.conclusion: The precautionary principle is part of domestic environmental law and requires anticipation of environmental harm and measures to avoid it, or selection of the least environmentally harmful activity, despite incomplete scientific certainty.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India, which recognized the precautionary principle as part of Indian environmental law, and on Articles 47, 48-A and 51-A(g) of the Constitution and environmental legislation including the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It also referred to Principle 15 of the Rio Declaration and the shift from the assimilative-capacity approach reflected in the Stockholm Declaration to the precautionary approach.

predicates.environmental_decision: A court, tribunal, authority or public decision-maker is deciding a matter concerning environmental protection or pollution.
predicates.serious_or_irreversible_harm_threat: The proposed activity presents a threat of serious or irreversible harm to the environment or human health.
predicates.scientific_uncertainty: Available scientific information is incomplete or uncertain about the likelihood or effects of the threatened harm.

issues.definition: When an environmental decision involves a threat of serious or irreversible harm and scientific uncertainty, the decision-maker must apply precautionary measures.

issues.legal_issue: A party proposing an activity that may harm the environment must bear the burden of showing that it presents no reasonable ecological or medical concern when the activity would alter the status quo amid a non-negligible environmental risk.
material_facts: An industry sought permission to establish a facility in a sensitive water-supply catchment area.
The pollution potential and effects of the proposed facility were disputed, and the court identified scientific uncertainty as a recurring feature of environmental cases.
The proposed activity would change the existing environmental conditions, while those seeking to preserve them would otherwise have faced the evidentiary burden.
issues.conclusion: The burden of proof in an environmental case falls on the actor or developer proposing to alter the status quo to show that the proposed action is environmentally benign; where the evidence does not alleviate reasonable concern, the presumption operates in favour of environmental protection.
issues.legal_principle: The court elaborated the special burden of proof recognized in Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India. It linked the burden to the precautionary principle and explained that, where environmental risks from inaction are uncertain but non-negligible, the proponent must show the absence of reasonable ecological or medical concern. It referred to the reasonable-person test and the discussion in Ashburton Acclimatisation Society v. Federated Farmers of New Zealand.

predicates.environmental_proceeding: A court or tribunal is dealing with a proceeding concerning environmental harm or protection.
predicates.proponent_seeks_to_change_status_quo: A person or entity proposes an activity that would alter the existing environmental conditions.
predicates.potential_environmental_risk_is_non_negl: The proposed activity presents a risk of environmental or human-health harm that is uncertain but not negligible.

issues.definition: In an environmental proceeding, a proponent seeking to alter the status quo amid a non-negligible potential risk must show that no reasonable environmental concern remains.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional court may obtain investigation and expert opinion from a suitably constituted statutory environmental authority on complex scientific or technical issues in an environmental case, while retaining control over the case and the authority’s opinion.
material_facts: The appeals and related proceedings raised complex scientific and technical disputes about an industry’s pollution potential and effects on a sensitive catchment area.
The court considered that ordinary judicial processes could have difficulty resolving such technical disputes promptly and adequately.
The statutory environmental appellate authority had a retired Supreme Court judge or Chief Justice and members with technical environmental expertise.
The parties agreed that specified questions about the industry’s hazardous character and its effects on the catchment area could be referred to that authority.
issues.conclusion: The court held that it could refer scientific and technical aspects of environmental cases arising before it or a High Court to the statutory environmental appellate authority for investigation and opinion; the opinion remains subject to the court’s approval. It referred the specified questions to the authority and left the question of trial runs for the authority to decide after hearing the parties.
issues.legal_principle: Relying on Paramjit Kaur v. State of Punjab, the court held that it could seek the assistance of an expert statutory body acting in aid of the court, without conferring new jurisdiction on that body and without relinquishing the court’s seisin or control. The court treated environmental concerns as connected to the right to life under Article 21 and referred to the National Environmental Appellate Authority Act, 1997, under which the authority included judicial and technical expertise.

predicates.environmental_constitutional_proceeding: A proceeding concerning environmental matters is before a constitutional court.
predicates.complex_scientific_or_technical_issue: Resolving the environmental dispute requires assessment of complex scientific or technical matters.
predicates.suitable_expert_authority_available: A statutory authority with appropriate judicial and technical expertise is available to investigate the issue and provide an opinion.

issues.definition: When a constitutional environmental proceeding involves a complex scientific or technical issue and a suitable expert authority is available, the court may refer the issue for investigation and opinion while retaining approval over the result.

issues.legal_issue: Environmental appellate authorities and tribunals should combine substantial judicial expertise with high-level scientific or technical expertise to adjudicate complex environmental disputes fairly and effectively.
material_facts: Environmental proceedings commonly require the evaluation of complex scientific and technological evidence.
The court identified environmental appellate bodies whose governing provisions did not clearly ensure an appropriate combination of judicial and technical expertise.
The appellate authority involved in this dispute was a retired judge without a technical member to assist on scientific matters.
The court considered that adjudication by bodies lacking either judicial or scientific expertise could undermine the purpose of environmental legislation.
issues.conclusion: The court stated that environmental courts, tribunals and appellate authorities should include a sitting or retired High Court or Supreme Court judge and experienced scientists or technical members, and urged the Central and State Governments to take appropriate legislative or other action to secure that composition.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the good-governance principle and its earlier observations in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Shriram Foods & Fertilizers case) and Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India concerning judicial and technical participation in environmental decision-making. It discussed section 28 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, section 31 of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, rule 12 of the Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 1989, section 10 of the National Environment Tribunal Act, 1995, and the National Environmental Appellate Authority Act, 1997. It also stated that such bodies should not be confined to Wednesbury-style limitations.

predicates.environmental_adjudicatory_body: A court, tribunal or appellate authority is constituted to decide environmental disputes.
predicates.complex_environmental_disputes_with_scie: The disputes the body must decide require assessment of complex environmental science or technology.

issues.definition: An environmental adjudicatory body facing complex scientific or technical disputes should include senior judicial expertise and experienced scientific or technical expertise.
